questions.question: A company is running a large web application that needs to always be available. The application tends to slow down when CPU usage is greater than 60%. How can they track when CPU usage goes above 60% for any of the EC2 Instances in their account?

options.text: Use CloudFront to monitor the CPU usage.

explanation.summary: Amazon CloudFront does not monitor EC2 instance CPU utilization.
explanation.why: CloudFront is a content delivery network designed to cache and deliver content from edge locations to reduce latency and improve performance for end users. It operates at the network and application delivery layer and has no visibility into EC2 instance-level metrics such as CPU utilization, memory usage, or disk I/O. Monitoring EC2 performance requires a service that collects and evaluates instance metrics, which CloudFront does not provide.

options.text: Set the AWS Config CPU threshold to 60% to receive a notification when EC2 usage exceeds that value.

explanation.summary: AWS Config does not monitor real-time performance metrics such as CPU utilization.
explanation.why: AWS Config is used to record, evaluate, and audit resource configurations and compliance against rules. It tracks configuration changes over time, such as whether an EC2 instance has public access or whether encryption is enabled. AWS Config does not collect or evaluate performance metrics like CPU usage and cannot trigger alerts based on utilization thresholds.

options.text: Use CloudWatch Alarms to monitor the CPUand alert when the CPU usage is >= 60%.

explanation.summary: Amazon CloudWatch Alarms can monitor EC2 CPU utilization metrics and trigger alerts when thresholds are exceeded.
keyPoints: Amazon EC2 publishes CPU utilization metrics automatically to Amazon CloudWatch
CloudWatch Alarms evaluate metrics against defined thresholds in near real time
Alarms can trigger notifications or automated actions when conditions are met
CPUUtilization is a standard EC2 metric available without additional configuration
Alarms can be applied to individual instances or groups of instances
examples: Creating a CloudWatch Alarm that triggers when CPUUtilization exceeds 60% for five consecutive minutes
Sending an SNS notification to operations teams when CPU usage crosses the threshold
Triggering Auto Scaling actions based on CloudWatch Alarm state changes
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon CloudWatch is the primary monitoring and observability service for AWS resources. EC2 instances automatically send basic metrics such as CPUUtilization, NetworkIn, NetworkOut, and DiskReadOps to CloudWatch at five-minute intervals, with optional one-minute granularity using detailed monitoring. CloudWatch Alarms continuously evaluate these metrics and transition between OK, ALARM, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA states based on defined conditions. When CPU usage exceeds a specified threshold, alarms can notify administrators via Amazon SNS, invoke AWS Lambda functions, or initiate Auto Scaling actions. This makes CloudWatch Alarms essential for maintaining high availability and performance in production environments, especially for applications sensitive to resource saturation.

options.text: Use SNS to menitor the utilization of the server.

explanation.summary: Amazon SNS delivers notifications but does not monitor server utilization.
explanation.why: Amazon Simple Notification Service is a messaging service used to send notifications to subscribers through email, SMS, HTTP endpoints, or other services. SNS does not collect metrics or evaluate performance thresholds. It is commonly used as a notification target for CloudWatch Alarms, but it cannot monitor CPU usage on its own.

questions.question: What is the recommended storage option when hosting an often-changing database on an Amazon EC2 instance?

explanation.summary: Amazon EBS is the recommended storage option for frequently changing databases running on EC2 instances.
keyPoints: Provides persistent block-level storage for EC2 instances
Optimized for low-latency and high-throughput workloads
Supports frequent read and write operations
Data persists independently of the EC2 instance lifecycle
Commonly used for databases and transactional workloads
examples: Running a MySQL or PostgreSQL database on EC2 with data stored on an EBS volume
Using provisioned IOPS EBS volumes for performance-sensitive database workloads
Attaching multiple EBS volumes to separate database logs and data files
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon Elastic Block Store is designed to behave like a traditional disk drive for EC2 instances. It offers consistent and predictable performance, making it ideal for databases that require frequent updates, low latency, and durability. EBS volumes are replicated within the same Availability Zone to protect against hardware failures, ensuring data durability. Unlike instance store volumes, EBS data persists even if the instance is stopped or terminated. While managed database services like Amazon RDS simplify operations, when a database is hosted directly on EC2, Amazon EBS is the correct and recommended storage layer.

explanation.summary: Amazon RDS is a managed database service, not a storage option for databases hosted on EC2.
explanation.why: Amazon RDS abstracts away the underlying infrastructure and does not expose storage management to the customer. While it is an excellent choice for managed databases, it does not apply when the database is explicitly hosted on an EC2 instance, where storage must be attached and managed separately.

options.text: You can't run a database inside an Amazon EC2 instance.

explanation.summary: Databases can be fully managed and run on Amazon EC2 instances.
explanation.why: Amazon EC2 provides full control over the operating system and installed software, allowing customers to install and manage any database engine they choose. Many organizations run self-managed relational and NoSQL databases on EC2 for customization or compatibility reasons.

explanation.summary: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed NoSQL database service, not storage for databases running on EC2.
explanation.why: DynamoDB is a serverless key-value and document database that does not rely on EC2 instances. It replaces the need to manage database servers rather than acting as attached storage for them.

questions.question: You are working as a site reliability engineer (SRE) in an AWS environment, which of the following services helps monitor your applications?

explanation.summary: Amazon CloudWatch is the primary service for monitoring applications and infrastructure in AWS.
keyPoints: Collects metrics, logs, and events from AWS services and applications
Provides real-time visibility into system performance and health
Supports alarms, dashboards, and automated actions
Integrates with EC2, Lambda, RDS, and many other services
Foundational tool for reliability and operational monitoring
examples: Monitoring application latency and error rates using CloudWatch metrics
Analyzing application logs stored in CloudWatch Logs
Creating dashboards to visualize system health across environments
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon CloudWatch is a core observability service that enables SRE teams to monitor, analyze, and respond to system behavior. It collects metrics from AWS resources automatically and allows custom metrics from applications. CloudWatch Logs provide centralized log storage and querying capabilities, while CloudWatch Alarms enable proactive alerting based on thresholds. CloudWatch Events and EventBridge allow event-driven automation in response to system changes. Together, these capabilities support reliability engineering practices such as monitoring service-level indicators, detecting anomalies, and responding quickly to incidents.

explanation.summary: Amazon CloudSearch is used for search functionality, not application monitoring.
explanation.why: CloudSearch is a managed search service designed to index and search application data. It does not collect metrics, logs, or health information about applications or infrastructure.

explanation.summary: Amazon EMR is a big data processing service, not a monitoring solution.
explanation.why: Amazon EMR is used to run large-scale data processing frameworks such as Hadoop and Spark. It does not provide observability or monitoring capabilities for general-purpose applications.

explanation.summary: Amazon CloudHSM is a hardware security module service, not a monitoring tool.
explanation.why: CloudHSM provides dedicated hardware appliances to manage cryptographic keys and perform encryption operations. It does not collect or analyze application performance or health data.

questions.question: What factors determine how you are charged when using AWS Lambda? (Choose TWO)

explanation.summary: AWS Lambda pricing is not based on storage consumption.
explanation.why: Lambda functions do not charge based on how much storage is used. While Lambda provides temporary storage in the /tmp directory and uses deployment package storage behind the scenes, customers are not billed based on storage size. Pricing is instead driven by request volume and execution duration.

options.text: Number of requests to your functions.

explanation.summary: AWS Lambda charges based on the number of requests made to a function.
keyPoints: Each invocation of a Lambda function counts as a request
Charges apply regardless of whether the invocation succeeds or fails
The free tier includes a large number of monthly requests
Request-based pricing applies across all invocation sources
Request charges are independent of execution duration
examples: A Lambda function invoked by API Gateway 5 million times in a month incurs request charges
Scheduled Lambda functions triggered every minute contribute to total request count
explanation.additionalInfo: AWS Lambda pricing includes a per-request charge that applies to every function invocation. This applies whether the function is triggered by API Gateway, S3 events, EventBridge schedules, or direct invocation. The AWS free tier provides 1 million free requests per month, after which charges apply per additional million requests. This model aligns Lambda costs directly with usage, making it cost effective for sporadic or event-driven workloads.

explanation.summary: Lambda pricing is not affected by the number of volumes.
explanation.why: AWS Lambda does not use or attach storage volumes such as Amazon EBS. Volumes are associated with EC2 instances, not serverless Lambda functions, making this option unrelated to Lambda billing.

explanation.summary: Placement groups are an EC2 feature and do not affect Lambda pricing.
explanation.why: Placement groups control how EC2 instances are placed on underlying hardware to optimize performance or availability. Lambda functions do not run on customer-managed instances and therefore are not impacted by placement groups.

explanation.summary: AWS Lambda charges based on the amount of compute time consumed during function execution.
keyPoints: Compute cost is calculated from execution duration
Duration is measured from function start to termination
Pricing scales with allocated memory size
Execution time is billed in millisecond increments
Longer-running functions incur higher compute charges
examples: A function running for 500 ms with 512 MB of memory incurs compute charges
Optimizing code to reduce execution time lowers Lambda costs
explanation.additionalInfo: Compute time is the second major component of AWS Lambda pricing. Charges are based on the configured memory size and the duration of execution. AWS bills in millisecond increments, encouraging efficient code and right-sized memory allocation. Increasing memory also increases CPU allocation, which can reduce execution time and sometimes lower overall cost. This pricing model reinforces serverless best practices of efficiency and event-driven design.

questions.question: What are the main differences between an IAM user and an IAM role in AWS? (Choose TWO)

options.text: An IAM user is uniquely associated with only one person, however a role is intended to be assumable by anyone who needs it.

explanation.summary: IAM users represent individual identities, while IAM roles are designed to be assumed by multiple entities.
keyPoints: IAM users are created for specific individuals or applications
Users have a fixed identity within an AWS account
IAM roles are not tied to a single person
Roles can be assumed by users, services, or external identities
examples: Creating an IAM user for a developer with personal credentials
Allowing multiple EC2 instances to assume the same IAM role
explanation.additionalInfo: IAM users are long-term identities that map directly to a single person or application. In contrast, IAM roles are intended to be assumed dynamically and can be used by AWS services, IAM users, or federated identities. This design enables scalable and secure access management without sharing credentials, which is a core AWS security best practice.

options.text: An IAM user has permanent credentials associated with it, however a role has temporary credentials associated with it.

explanation.summary: IAM users use long-term credentials, while IAM roles issue temporary credentials.
keyPoints: IAM users use access keys or passwords that do not expire automatically
IAM roles rely on AWS Security Token Service (STS)
Role credentials are temporary and automatically rotated
Temporary credentials reduce the risk of credential leakage
Roles eliminate the need to store long-term secrets
examples: Using STS AssumeRole to obtain temporary credentials
An EC2 instance using role credentials that rotate automatically
explanation.additionalInfo: The distinction between long-term and temporary credentials is fundamental to AWS security. IAM user credentials remain valid until rotated or revoked, while IAM role credentials are time-limited and managed by AWS STS. This makes roles safer for automation, cross-account access, and service-to-service communication. AWS strongly recommends using roles wherever possible instead of embedding access keys.

options.text: IAM users are more cost effective than IAM roles.

explanation.summary: IAM users and IAM roles do not have cost differences.
explanation.why: AWS Identity and Access Management does not charge for creating users or roles. Cost effectiveness is not a distinguishing factor between the two.

options.text: Arole is uniquely associated with only one person, however an IAM user is intended to be assumable by anyone who needs it.

explanation.summary: This statement reverses the correct relationship between users and roles.
explanation.why: IAM users are associated with individual identities, while IAM roles are designed to be assumed by multiple entities. This option incorrectly swaps those definitions.

options.text: An IAM user has temporary credentials associated withit, however a role has permanent credentials associated with it.

explanation.summary: This option incorrectly describes credential behavior in IAM.
explanation.why: IAM users use long-term credentials, while IAM roles use temporary credentials provided by AWS STS. The statement reverses this behavior and is therefore incorrect.

questions.question: Which of the following actions may reduce Amazon EBS costs? (Choose TWO)

explanation.summary: Deleting unused buckets affects S3 costs, not EBS costs.
explanation.why: Amazon S3 buckets are a separate storage service from Amazon EBS. Removing unused S3 buckets reduces S3 storage costs but has no impact on EBS volumes or snapshot charges.

explanation.summary: Reservations apply to compute services, not Amazon EBS storage.
explanation.why: Reserved Instances and Savings Plans reduce EC2 compute costs. Amazon EBS pricing is based on provisioned storage and snapshots and does not support reservations.

explanation.summary: Deleting unused EBS snapshots reduces ongoing snapshot storage charges.
keyPoints: EBS snapshots are stored in Amazon S3 and billed incrementally
Unused snapshots continue to incur storage costs
Deleting old snapshots frees billed storage space
Incremental snapshot behavior can lead to hidden costs
Lifecycle policies help automate snapshot cleanup
examples: Removing obsolete backup snapshots no longer required for recovery
Using Data Lifecycle Manager to delete snapshots after retention period
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon EBS snapshots are incremental, meaning each snapshot only stores changed blocks. However, deleting an EBS volume does not automatically delete its snapshots. Orphaned snapshots can accumulate and generate ongoing costs. Regular review and cleanup of snapshots is a common and effective cost-optimization strategy. AWS Data Lifecycle Manager can automate snapshot creation and deletion based on retention rules.

options.text: Changing the type of the volume.

explanation.summary: Selecting a more cost-effective EBS volume type can reduce storage costs.
keyPoints: Different EBS volume types have different pricing
Some workloads do not require high-performance volumes
Volumes can be modified without downtime in many cases
Cost optimization depends on workload requirements
examples: Migrating from Provisioned IOPS SSD to General Purpose SSD
Switching to HDD volumes for infrequently accessed data
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon EBS offers multiple volume types optimized for different performance and cost characteristics. Over-provisioning high-performance volumes leads to unnecessary cost. AWS allows volume type modification without detaching the volume in most cases, enabling customers to optimize costs without disruption. Selecting the correct volume type based on IOPS and throughput requirements is a key storage cost optimization practice.

explanation.summary: Distributing requests improves performance but does not directly reduce EBS costs.
explanation.why: Spreading I/O across multiple volumes can improve throughput and fault tolerance but may increase overall storage costs. Cost reduction focuses on storage size, volume type, and snapshot management, not request distribution.

questions.question: What does Amazon GuardDuty do to protect AWS accounts and workloads?

options.text: Notifies AWS customers about abuse events once they are reported.

explanation.summary: Amazon GuardDuty does not rely on externally reported abuse events.
explanation.why: GuardDuty is a continuous threat detection service that proactively analyzes data sources such as CloudTrail logs, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs. It does not wait for abuse reports or customer notifications to identify threats. Its value lies in near real-time detection based on behavioral analysis and threat intelligence.

options.text: Continuously monitors AWS infrastructure and helps detect threats such as attacker reconnaissance or account compromise.

explanation.summary: Amazon GuardDuty continuously monitors AWS environments to detect malicious or unauthorized activity.
keyPoints: Analyzes CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs
Uses machine learning and threat intelligence feeds
Detects reconnaissance, credential compromise, and lateral movement
Provides actionable security findings with severity levels
Requires no additional software or agents
examples: Detecting API calls from anomalous geographic locations
Identifying port scanning activity against EC2 instances
Flagging compromised IAM credentials used for unusual behavior
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon GuardDuty is a fully managed threat detection service designed to improve security posture with minimal operational overhead. It continuously evaluates multiple AWS-native telemetry sources to identify suspicious patterns indicative of attacks. GuardDuty findings include detailed context such as affected resources, attack vectors, and recommended remediation steps. Because it operates without agents and requires minimal configuration, GuardDuty is commonly enabled by default in security-focused AWS environments. It integrates with EventBridge and Security Hub to support automated response and centralized security management.

options.text: Helps AWS customers identify the root cause of potential security issues.

explanation.summary: GuardDuty detects threats but does not perform root cause analysis.
explanation.why: While GuardDuty provides detailed findings, root cause analysis is typically performed by security teams using logs, timelines, and forensic tools. GuardDuty highlights suspicious activity but does not determine organizational or process-level root causes.

options.text: Checks security groups for rules that allow unrestricted access to AWS. resources.

explanation.summary: Security group rule analysis is not performed by GuardDuty.
explanation.why: Identifying overly permissive security group rules is handled by services such as AWS Trusted Advisor or AWS Config. GuardDuty focuses on detecting malicious behavior rather than static configuration analysis.

questions.question: Which database service should you use if your application and data schema require 'joins' or complex transactions?

explanation.summary: Amazon RDS supports relational databases that handle joins and complex transactions.
keyPoints: Common choice for structured relational data
examples: Using MySQL on Amazon RDS for transactional applications
Running PostgreSQL workloads requiring foreign key constraints
Handling multi-table joins for reporting queries
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon Relational Database Service is designed for workloads that require strong consistency, structured schemas, and complex relationships between data entities. Relational engines such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server provide full SQL support, including joins, stored procedures, and transactional guarantees. AWS manages the underlying infrastructure, automating backups, patching, and failover, allowing customers to focus on application logic rather than database maintenance.

explanation.summary: AWS Outposts is an infrastructure service, not a database service.
explanation.why: AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure to on-premises environments but does not provide database functionality itself. Databases must still be deployed on supported services running on Outposts.

explanation.summary: Amazon DocumentDB is designed for document-based workloads, not relational joins.
explanation.why: DocumentDB is a NoSQL document database compatible with MongoDB APIs. It does not support relational joins or complex SQL transactions, making it unsuitable for workloads that require relational data models.

explanation.summary: Amazon DynamoDB does not support relational joins or complex transactions.
explanation.why: DynamoDB is a key-value and document database optimized for high scalability and low latency. It does not support SQL joins and is not intended for complex relational transaction processing.

questions.question: Which of the following makes it easier for you to categorize, manage and filter your resources?

explanation.summary: Amazon CloudWatch is a monitoring service, not a resource categorization tool.
explanation.why: CloudWatch collects metrics, logs, and events for observability. It does not provide mechanisms for tagging or categorizing AWS resources for management or cost allocation purposes.

explanation.summary: AWS Service Catalog manages approved products, not resource categorization.
explanation.why: Service Catalog helps organizations manage and govern IT services that users can deploy. It does not provide tagging or filtering across existing AWS resources.

explanation.summary: AWS Directory Service provides managed directories, not resource tagging.
explanation.why: Directory Service integrates with Microsoft Active Directory for identity management. It does not categorize or manage AWS resources.

explanation.summary: AWS Tagging allows resources to be labeled for easier organization and management.
keyPoints: Tags are key-value pairs assigned to AWS resources
Enable filtering and grouping of resources
Support cost allocation and chargeback models
examples: Tagging resources by environment such as dev, test, and production
Using cost allocation tags for billing analysis
Filtering resources by owner or project
explanation.additionalInfo: AWS Tagging is a foundational management practice that enables visibility, governance, and cost control across AWS environments. Tags are applied as metadata and can be used by AWS services, the Management Console, CLI, and APIs to filter, group, and automate actions on resources. Tag-based access control allows IAM policies to restrict actions based on resource tags. Cost allocation tags enable detailed billing analysis and accountability. Consistent tagging strategies are critical in large or multi-account AWS environments.

questions.question: What should you consider when storing data in Amazon Glacier?

options.text: Amazon Glacier only accepts data in a compressed format.

explanation.summary: Amazon Glacier does not require data to be stored in a compressed format.
explanation.why: Amazon Glacier accepts data in its original form. While customers may choose to compress data to reduce storage costs, compression is optional and not enforced by the service.

options.text: Glacier can only be used to store frequently accessed data and data archives.

explanation.summary: Amazon Glacier is not intended for frequently accessed data.
explanation.why: Glacier is designed for long-term archival storage where data is accessed infrequently. Retrieval times can range from minutes to hours, making it unsuitable for frequent access patterns.

options.text: Amazon Glacier does not provide immediate retrieval of data.

explanation.summary: Amazon Glacier is designed for low-cost archival storage with delayed retrieval times.
keyPoints: Retrieval can take minutes to hours depending on retrieval option
Lower cost compared to frequently accessed storage
Not suitable for real-time access workloads
Supports standard, expedited, and bulk retrieval options
examples: Storing compliance records that are accessed only during audits
Archiving historical log files for long-term retention
Keeping backups that are rarely restored
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon Glacier, now part of Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes, is designed for data that does not require immediate access. Retrieval times vary based on the retrieval tier selected, allowing customers to balance cost and access speed. This trade-off is fundamental to Glacier’s pricing model and is a key consideration when choosing it for archival workloads.

options.text: Attach Glacier to an EC2 Instance to be able to store data.

explanation.summary: Amazon Glacier is not attached to EC2 instances like block storage.
explanation.why: Glacier is an object storage service accessed through APIs and the S3 interface. It cannot be attached to EC2 instances as a filesystem or block device.

questions.question: Engineers are wasting a lot of time and effort managing batch computing software in traditional data centers. Which of the following AWS services allows them to easily run thousands of batch computing jobs?

explanation.summary: Amazon EC2 provides compute capacity but does not manage batch job scheduling.
explanation.why: While EC2 can be used to run batch workloads, customers would still need to manage job queues, scheduling, scaling, and retries themselves.

explanation.summary: AWS Batch is designed to run large-scale batch computing workloads efficiently.
keyPoints: Scales to thousands of batch jobs
Integrates with EC2 and Spot Instances
examples: Running large-scale scientific simulations
Processing financial risk calculations overnight
Executing media rendering or genomics workloads
explanation.additionalInfo: AWS Batch abstracts the complexity of running batch jobs by handling compute provisioning, job scheduling, retries, and scaling. Customers define job requirements, and AWS Batch determines the optimal resources to execute them. This significantly reduces operational overhead compared to managing batch systems in traditional data centers.

explanation.summary: Lambda@Edge is used for request processing at CloudFront edge locations.
explanation.why: Lambda@Edge runs lightweight functions in response to CDN events. It is not designed for large-scale batch processing or long-running jobs.

explanation.summary: AWS Fargate runs containers without managing servers but does not manage batch workflows.
explanation.why: Fargate provides serverless compute for containers but does not include native job scheduling, queueing, or batch orchestration features.

questions.question: How can you increase your application's fault-tolerance while it is being hosted in AWS?

options.text: Deploy your application across multiple EC2 instances.

explanation.summary: Using multiple EC2 instances alone does not guarantee fault tolerance.
explanation.why: If all instances are deployed within a single Availability Zone, failures at the zone level can still impact the entire application.

options.text: Deploy your application across multiple Availability Zones.

explanation.summary: Deploying across multiple Availability Zones increases fault tolerance.
keyPoints: Availability Zones are isolated from each other
examples: Running EC2 instances in at least two Availability Zones
Using Elastic Load Balancing across zones
Deploying databases with Multi-AZ configurations
explanation.additionalInfo: Fault tolerance in AWS is achieved by designing systems that can withstand failures of individual components. Availability Zones are physically separated locations within a region with independent power, networking, and cooling. Deploying resources across multiple AZs ensures that a failure in one zone does not bring down the entire application, making this a core principle of highly available AWS architectures.

options.text: Host your application on one powerful EC2 instance type instead of multiple smaller instances.

explanation.summary: A single large instance introduces a single point of failure.
explanation.why: Relying on one instance, regardless of size, reduces fault tolerance and increases risk of downtime if that instance fails.

options.text: Deploy the underlying application resources across multiple subnets.

explanation.summary: Multiple subnets alone do not guarantee fault tolerance.
explanation.why: Subnets can exist within the same Availability Zone. Without spanning multiple AZs, subnet distribution does not protect against zone-level failures.

questions.question: Which of the following AWS Support Plans gives you 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers via email & phone? (Choose TWO)

explanation.summary: The Developer Support plan does not provide 24/7 phone access to Cloud Support Engineers.
explanation.why: The Developer plan offers business-hours email access only and is intended for non-production or early development workloads. It does not include phone support or 24/7 availability.

explanation.summary: Premium is not an official AWS Support Plan name.
explanation.why: AWS offers Basic, Developer, Business, and Enterprise support plans. Premium is not a valid plan and therefore cannot provide any support features.

explanation.summary: The Enterprise Support plan provides 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers via phone and email.
keyPoints: Includes 24/7 phone, chat, and email support
Provides access to a Technical Account Manager
Includes proactive guidance and architecture reviews
examples: Enterprise customers calling AWS Support during a critical outage
Using a Technical Account Manager for proactive operational planning
explanation.additionalInfo: The AWS Enterprise Support plan is intended for large-scale, business-critical workloads that require rapid response and deep AWS expertise. It offers 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers through multiple channels and includes a dedicated Technical Account Manager who provides proactive support, architectural guidance, and operational reviews. This plan is commonly required for enterprises with strict uptime and compliance requirements.

explanation.summary: Standard is not an AWS Support Plan.
explanation.why: AWS does not offer a support plan called Standard. The official plans are Basic, Developer, Business, and Enterprise.

explanation.summary: The Business Support plan provides 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers via phone and email.
keyPoints: Includes 24/7 phone, chat, and email support
Provides faster response times than Developer plan
Includes guidance for architecture and best practices
Commonly used by growing production environments
examples: Operations teams contacting AWS Support during off-hours incidents
Using Business support for architectural troubleshooting
explanation.additionalInfo: AWS Business Support is suitable for customers running production workloads that require round-the-clock assistance. While it does not include a dedicated Technical Account Manager like the Enterprise plan, it still provides 24/7 access to Cloud Support Engineers and significantly faster response times than the Developer plan. This makes it a common choice for mid-sized production environments.

questions.question: Which of the following requires an access key ID and a secret access key to get long-lived programmatic access to AWS resources? (Choose TWO)

explanation.summary: IAM groups do not have credentials.
explanation.why: IAM groups are used to manage permissions for multiple users. They cannot authenticate or make API calls and therefore do not use access keys.

explanation.summary: IAM users use access key ID and secret access key for long-lived programmatic access.
keyPoints: Access keys belong to IAM users
Used for AWS CLI, SDKs, and API calls
Must be protected and rotated regularly
Not recommended for use when roles are possible
examples: Configuring AWS CLI with an IAM user's access keys
Application using SDK credentials tied to an IAM user
explanation.additionalInfo: IAM users can be assigned access key pairs that allow programmatic access to AWS services. These credentials remain valid until explicitly rotated or deleted, which makes them long-lived. Because long-lived credentials increase security risk, AWS recommends using IAM roles with temporary credentials wherever possible.

explanation.summary: IAM roles do not use long-lived access keys.
explanation.why: IAM roles rely on temporary credentials issued by AWS STS. They do not have permanent access keys associated with them.

explanation.summary: The AWS root user can have long-lived access keys.
keyPoints: Root user can create access key pairs
Use of root access keys is strongly discouraged
examples: Root access keys created during early account setup
Security teams rotating root credentials after exposure risk
explanation.additionalInfo: The AWS account root user can generate access key ID and secret access key pairs that provide full, unrestricted access to the account. Because these credentials bypass all IAM permission boundaries, AWS strongly recommends disabling or deleting root access keys and using IAM users and roles instead. MFA should always be enabled on the root account to reduce risk.

explanation.summary: A Technical Account Manager does not provide programmatic access credentials.
explanation.why: A TAM is an AWS support role assigned to Enterprise customers and is not an IAM identity or authentication mechanism.

questions.question: Which of the following is a benefit of the 'Loose Coupling' architecture principle?

options.text: It eliminates the need for change management.

explanation.summary: Loose coupling does not eliminate the need for change management.
explanation.why: Even loosely coupled systems require governance, versioning, and controlled deployments to ensure stability and compatibility.

explanation.summary: Cross-Region Replication is not a direct benefit of loose coupling.
explanation.why: Replication strategies are storage or service features. Loose coupling focuses on minimizing dependencies between components.

options.text: It helps AWS customers reduce Privileged Access to AWS resources.

explanation.summary: Reducing privileged access is a security practice, not a core benefit of loose coupling.
explanation.why: Loose coupling improves system resilience and flexibility, not identity and access management.

options.text: It allows individual application compenents or services to be modified without affecting other components.

explanation.summary: Loose coupling allows components to change independently.
keyPoints: Reduces blast radius of changes or failures
examples: Updating a payment service without redeploying the frontend
Replacing a backend service without impacting consumers
explanation.additionalInfo: Loose coupling is a core cloud architecture principle that enables agility and resilience. By designing components to interact through well-defined interfaces and asynchronous communication, changes in one component do not cascade to others. This allows faster innovation, safer deployments, and improved fault isolation, all of which are essential for scalable cloud-native systems.

questions.question: A company needs to host a big data application on AWS using EC2 instances. Which of the following AWS Storage services would they choose to automatically get high throughput to multiple compute nodes?

explanation.summary: Amazon EBS is block storage designed for a single EC2 instance at a time.
explanation.why: EBS volumes are attached to individual EC2 instances and are not designed to be shared concurrently across multiple compute nodes. While EBS provides high performance for single-instance workloads, it does not support the shared, scalable access patterns required for big data workloads running across many EC2 instances.

explanation.summary: AWS Storage Gateway is used for hybrid storage, not high-throughput shared compute access.
explanation.why: Storage Gateway connects on-premises environments to AWS storage services. It is not optimized for high-performance shared access by multiple EC2 instances in a big data processing environment.

explanation.summary: Amazon EFS provides scalable, shared file storage with high throughput for multiple EC2 instances.
keyPoints: Designed for concurrent access by thousands of EC2 instances
Automatically scales throughput based on workload
Ideal for big data and analytics workloads
examples: Running Hadoop or Spark clusters with shared datasets
Multiple EC2 instances processing the same data files concurrently
Big data analytics workloads requiring high aggregate throughput
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon Elastic File System is a fully managed, scalable NFS file system designed for use with AWS compute services. EFS automatically grows and shrinks as files are added or removed and scales throughput based on usage patterns. Because it supports concurrent access from many EC2 instances, it is well suited for big data workloads, analytics pipelines, and distributed processing frameworks that require shared access to large datasets.

explanation.summary: Amazon S3 is object storage and does not provide a shared file system interface.
explanation.why: S3 offers massive scalability and durability but is accessed via object APIs rather than a POSIX-compatible file system. Many big data frameworks can use S3, but when a shared file system with automatic high throughput across compute nodes is required, EFS is the appropriate choice.

questions.question: Which of the following Cloud Computing deployment models eliminates the need to run and maintain physical data centers?

explanation.summary: On-premises deployments require full ownership and maintenance of physical infrastructure.
explanation.why: In an on-premises model, the organization is responsible for procuring, operating, and maintaining all hardware, networking, power, and cooling resources.

explanation.summary: IaaS still relies on cloud infrastructure but does not describe a full deployment model by itself.
explanation.why: Infrastructure as a Service defines a service category, not the overarching deployment model that removes data center ownership. The broader cloud deployment model encompasses IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.

explanation.summary: PaaS abstracts infrastructure management but does not define the overall deployment model.
explanation.why: Platform as a Service removes server management responsibilities but still operates within the cloud deployment model rather than defining it.

explanation.summary: The cloud deployment model removes the need to operate physical data centers.
keyPoints: AWS manages data centers, power, and cooling
examples: Running applications entirely on AWS-managed infrastructure
Scaling workloads globally without building data centers
explanation.additionalInfo: The cloud deployment model shifts infrastructure ownership and management to the cloud provider. Customers consume compute, storage, and networking resources as services without maintaining physical facilities. This allows organizations to focus on application development and business outcomes rather than data center operations.

questions.question: What are the benefits of the AWS Marketplace service? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Protects customers by performing periodic security checks on listed products.

explanation.summary: AWS Marketplace performs security and compliance reviews on listed products.
keyPoints: Reduces risk when deploying third-party software
examples: Selecting pre-approved AMIs from AWS Marketplace
Deploying security-reviewed SaaS solutions
explanation.additionalInfo: AWS Marketplace includes security and compliance checks to ensure listed products meet AWS standards. This reduces customer risk when adopting third-party solutions and accelerates deployment by providing trusted, vetted offerings.

explanation.summary: Per-second billing is not a general benefit of AWS Marketplace.
explanation.why: Billing granularity depends on the specific product and underlying AWS service, not the Marketplace itself.

options.text: Provides cheaper options for purchasing Amazon EC2 on-demand instances.

explanation.summary: EC2 pricing is not discounted through AWS Marketplace.
explanation.why: AWS Marketplace provides software solutions, not discounted EC2 pricing options.

options.text: Provides flexible pricing options that suit most customer needs.

explanation.summary: AWS Marketplace offers flexible pricing models for software solutions.
keyPoints: Supports hourly, monthly, and annual pricing
examples: Paying hourly for a third-party firewall appliance
Using subscription-based SaaS through AWS Marketplace
explanation.additionalInfo: AWS Marketplace allows customers to choose from a wide range of pricing models, including hourly usage, subscriptions, and bring-your-own-license options. All charges appear on the AWS bill, simplifying cost management and procurement.

options.text: Provides software solutions that run on AWS or any other Cloud vendor.

explanation.summary: AWS Marketplace primarily provides solutions designed to run on AWS.
explanation.why: Most Marketplace products are optimized for AWS services and infrastructure. Cross-cloud compatibility is not a general benefit.

questions.question: What is the benefit of Amazon EBS volumes being automatically replicated within the same availability zone?

explanation.summary: Elasticity refers to scaling resources up or down, not data protection.
explanation.why: EBS replication within an Availability Zone is about protecting data against hardware failure, not dynamically scaling capacity or performance.

explanation.summary: Automatic replication within an Availability Zone increases data durability.
keyPoints: EBS data is replicated across multiple storage devices
examples: Recovering data transparently after a disk failure
Maintaining database integrity during hardware issues
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon EBS volumes are designed to be highly durable by automatically replicating data within the same Availability Zone. This replication protects against the failure of individual components such as disks or storage servers. While EBS does not protect against Availability Zone-level outages, it significantly reduces the risk of data loss due to hardware failure, making it suitable for mission-critical workloads.

explanation.summary: Traceability relates to tracking actions and changes, not storage replication.
explanation.why: Traceability is provided by logging services such as AWS CloudTrail, not by EBS replication mechanisms.

explanation.summary: Accessibility refers to access patterns, not data replication.
explanation.why: EBS replication improves durability but does not change how or where volumes are accessed.

questions.question: You are planning to launch an advertising campaign over the coming weekend to promote a new digital product. It is expected that there will be heavy spikes in load during the campaign period, and you can't afford any downtime. You need additional compute resources to handle the additional load. What is the most cost-effective EC2 instance purchasing option for this job?

explanation.summary: Savings Plans are designed for steady, long-term usage.
explanation.why: Savings Plans require a long-term commitment and are not optimal for short-lived, unpredictable workloads such as weekend campaigns.

explanation.summary: Spot Instances can be interrupted and do not guarantee availability.
explanation.why: Because the campaign cannot afford downtime, Spot Instances are unsuitable due to the risk of interruption when capacity is reclaimed by AWS.

explanation.summary: Reserved Instances are intended for predictable, long-term workloads.
explanation.why: Reserved Instances require a one- or three-year commitment, making them cost-inefficient for short, bursty usage.

explanation.summary: On-Demand Instances provide immediate capacity with no long-term commitment.
keyPoints: Ideal for short-term or unpredictable workloads
examples: Scaling web servers during a limited-time promotion
Handling unpredictable traffic spikes without pre-planning
explanation.additionalInfo: On-Demand Instances are the most cost-effective option for short-lived workloads where availability is critical and usage duration is uncertain. While they have a higher per-hour cost than reserved or spot instances, they avoid long-term commitments and interruption risks, making them ideal for temporary campaigns and burst traffic scenarios.

questions.question: Which of the following AWS services integrates with AWS Shield and AWS Web Application Firewall (AWS WAF) to protect against network and application layer DDoS attacks?

explanation.summary: Amazon EFS is a file storage service and does not provide DDoS protection.
explanation.why: EFS offers shared file storage and does not integrate with AWS Shield or AWS WAF.

explanation.summary: AWS Secrets Manager manages secrets, not network traffic protection.
explanation.why: Secrets Manager is used to store and rotate credentials and does not provide DDoS mitigation capabilities.

explanation.summary: AWS Systems Manager is an operations management service.
explanation.why: Systems Manager focuses on automation, patching, and configuration management, not DDoS protection.

explanation.summary: Amazon CloudFront integrates with AWS Shield and AWS WAF for DDoS protection.
keyPoints: Supports AWS WAF for application-layer protection
Absorbs and mitigates large-scale DDoS attacks
examples: Protecting a public website from volumetric attacks
Blocking malicious requests using WAF rules at the edge
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network that sits at the edge of the AWS network. By integrating with AWS Shield and AWS WAF, CloudFront helps protect applications against both network-layer and application-layer DDoS attacks. Shield provides automatic DDoS mitigation, while WAF allows fine-grained control over HTTP and HTTPS traffic. This combination is a recommended best practice for protecting internet-facing applications.

questions.question: Which of the following services is used when encrypting EBS volumes?

explanation.summary: AWS WAF protects web applications and does not perform encryption.
explanation.why: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that filters HTTP and HTTPS traffic. It does not manage encryption keys or perform encryption for storage services.

explanation.summary: AWS KMS manages the encryption keys used to encrypt Amazon EBS volumes.
keyPoints: Used for EBS encryption at rest
examples: Encrypting EBS volumes using an AWS-managed CMK
Using customer-managed CMKs for compliance requirements
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon EBS encryption uses AWS Key Management Service to generate and manage encryption keys. When EBS encryption is enabled, data is encrypted at rest, in transit between the volume and the instance, and during snapshots. AWS KMS provides fine-grained access control, audit logging through CloudTrail, and key rotation capabilities, making it a core security service for storage encryption.

explanation.summary: Amazon Macie identifies sensitive data but does not encrypt storage.
explanation.why: Macie is a data security and privacy service that discovers and classifies sensitive data in Amazon S3. It does not provide encryption capabilities for EBS volumes.

explanation.summary: Amazon GuardDuty detects threats but does not manage encryption.
explanation.why: GuardDuty analyzes logs to identify malicious activity. It does not provide encryption or key management services.

questions.question: The AWS account administrator of your company has been fired. With the permissions granted to him as an administrator, he was able to create multiple IAM user accounts and access keys. Additionally, you are not sure whether he has access to the AWS root account or not. What should you do immediately to protect your AWS infrastructure? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Download all the attached policies in a safe place.

explanation.summary: Downloading policies does not prevent unauthorized access.
explanation.why: Saving policy documents does not revoke credentials or block access. Immediate action is required to eliminate potential compromise.

options.text: Delete all IAM accounts and recreate them.

explanation.summary: Deleting all IAM users is disruptive and unnecessary.
explanation.why: Mass deletion risks breaking applications and services. Targeted credential rotation and account protection are more effective and immediate.

options.text: Use the CloudWatch service to check all API calls that have been made in your account since the administrator was fired.

explanation.summary: CloudWatch is not the primary service for auditing API calls.
explanation.why: AWS CloudTrail records API activity. While investigation is important, immediate protection requires access revocation and credential security.

explanation.summary: Rotating access keys immediately invalidates potentially compromised credentials.
keyPoints: Prevents use of stolen or exposed keys
Applies to IAM users and applications
Essential first step after personnel changes
examples: Rotating keys for all IAM users with programmatic access
Updating applications with new credentials after rotation
explanation.additionalInfo: Access key rotation is a critical incident response step when credential compromise is suspected. Rotating keys immediately invalidates old credentials and prevents unauthorized API access. AWS recommends regular rotation of access keys and using IAM roles with temporary credentials whenever possible to reduce reliance on long-lived keys.

options.text: Change the email address and password of the root user account and enable MFA.

explanation.summary: Securing the root account prevents unrestricted access to the AWS account.
examples: Resetting root credentials after admin departure
Enabling hardware or virtual MFA on the root account
explanation.additionalInfo: The AWS root user has unrestricted access to all resources in the account. If root credentials are compromised, the entire environment is at risk. Changing the root email, password, and enabling MFA immediately locks down this access path. AWS strongly recommends using the root account only for tasks that require it and protecting it with MFA at all times.

questions.question: What is the Amazon ElastiCache service used for? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Provide an in-memory data storage service.

explanation.summary: Amazon ElastiCache provides fully managed in-memory data stores.
keyPoints: Stores data in memory for low latency
examples: Caching frequently accessed database queries
Storing session data for web applications
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon ElastiCache is designed to deliver microsecond-level latency by storing data entirely in memory. It is commonly used to reduce database load, speed up dynamic web applications, and improve overall system performance. ElastiCache supports both Redis and Memcached, allowing customers to choose the engine that best fits their use case.

options.text: Reduce delivery costs using Edge Locations.

explanation.summary: Reducing delivery costs using edge locations is the function of Amazon CloudFront.
explanation.why: ElastiCache does not operate at edge locations and does not deliver content globally.

explanation.summary: ElastiCache improves application performance by reducing latency and backend load.
keyPoints: Serves frequently accessed data from memory
examples: Caching user profile data
Storing leaderboard or session information
explanation.additionalInfo: By caching frequently accessed data in memory, ElastiCache dramatically reduces the need to query slower disk-based databases. This leads to faster response times, improved scalability, and better user experience, especially during traffic spikes.

options.text: Provide a Chef-compatible cache to speed up application response.

explanation.summary: ElastiCache is not related to Chef configuration management.
explanation.why: Chef is a configuration management tool. ElastiCache provides in-memory data storage and caching, not configuration management.

explanation.summary: Request distribution is handled by load balancers, not ElastiCache.
explanation.why: Elastic Load Balancing distributes traffic across instances. ElastiCache focuses on data caching and storage.

questions.question: The elasticity of the AWS Cloud enables customers to save costs when compared to traditional hosting providers. What can AWS customers do to benefit from the elasticity of the AWS Cloud? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Deploy your resources across multiple Availability Zones.

explanation.summary: Using multiple Availability Zones improves availability, not elasticity-driven cost savings.
explanation.why: Multi-AZ deployments protect against failures but do not directly scale resources up or down based on demand, which is the core concept of elasticity.

explanation.summary: Auto Scaling adjusts compute capacity automatically based on demand.
keyPoints: Scales instances in and out automatically
examples: Scaling out EC2 instances during peak traffic
Scaling in overnight to reduce costs
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling is a primary elasticity feature in AWS. It allows customers to automatically add or remove EC2 instances based on defined metrics or schedules. This ensures applications have enough capacity during peak demand while minimizing cost during low usage periods.

options.text: Deploy your resources in another region.

explanation.summary: Multi-region deployment focuses on resilience, not elasticity.
explanation.why: Deploying resources in multiple regions improves disaster recovery and global reach but does not inherently scale capacity based on demand.

explanation.summary: Elastic Load Balancing distributes traffic but does not scale resources by itself.
explanation.why: While ELB works closely with Auto Scaling, it does not add or remove capacity on its own and therefore does not directly drive elasticity-based cost savings.

explanation.summary: Serverless services automatically scale with demand and charge only for usage.
keyPoints: No need to provision or manage servers
Pay only for execution time or requests
examples: Using AWS Lambda for event-driven workloads
Running APIs with Amazon API Gateway and Lambda
explanation.additionalInfo: Serverless computing services such as AWS Lambda, DynamoDB, and API Gateway scale automatically in response to demand. Customers are charged only for actual usage, making serverless a powerful way to benefit from AWS elasticity and significantly reduce costs compared to always-on infrastructure.

questions.question: What are some of the benefits of using On-Demand EC2 instances? (Choose TWO)

options.text: They provide free capacity when testing your new applications.

explanation.summary: On-Demand instances are billed from the moment they run.
explanation.why: AWS charges for On-Demand instances by the second or hour depending on the instance type. Free capacity is not a feature of On-Demand pricing.

options.text: They are cheaper than all other EC2 options.

explanation.summary: On-Demand instances are not the cheapest EC2 pricing option.
explanation.why: Spot Instances and Reserved pricing options offer lower costs but come with trade-offs such as interruptions or long-term commitments.

options.text: They remove the need to buy 'safety net' capacity to handle periodic traffic spikes.

explanation.summary: On-Demand instances allow scaling without pre-purchasing unused capacity.
examples: Launching extra instances during seasonal traffic
Scaling compute resources during flash sales
explanation.additionalInfo: On-Demand pricing eliminates the need to maintain idle capacity for peak traffic. Customers can scale up when needed and scale down when demand drops, paying only for the time instances are running.

options.text: They only require 1-2 days for setup and configuration.

explanation.summary: On-Demand instances are available immediately.
explanation.why: EC2 instances can be launched within minutes. Setup time is not a pricing benefit and is unrelated to On-Demand characteristics.

options.text: You can increase or decrease your compute capacity depending on the demands of your application.

explanation.summary: On-Demand instances provide flexible scaling without long-term commitments.
keyPoints: Scale up or down at any time
examples: Adding instances during peak hours
Reducing instance count during low usage periods
explanation.additionalInfo: The flexibility of On-Demand instances allows customers to respond immediately to changing workload demands. This elasticity is one of the primary benefits of the AWS Cloud and supports efficient resource utilization.

questions.question: Each AWS Region is composed of multiple Availability Zones. Which of the following best describes what an Availability Zone is?

options.text: It is a data center designed to be completely isolated from other data centers in the same region.

explanation.summary: An Availability Zone is not a single isolated data center.
explanation.why: Each Availability Zone consists of one or more data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity.

options.text: It is a collection of data centers distributed in multiple countries.

explanation.summary: Multiple countries describe regions, not Availability Zones.
explanation.why: Availability Zones are contained within a single region and do not span countries.

options.text: It is a logically isolated network of the AWS Cloud.

explanation.summary: Logical isolation describes a VPC, not an Availability Zone.
explanation.why: A VPC is a logically isolated network, while an Availability Zone is a physical location.

options.text: It is a distinct location within a region that is insulated from « failures in other Availability Zones.

explanation.summary: Availability Zones are isolated locations within a region designed to prevent cascading failures.
examples: Running application tiers across two Availability Zones
Failing over traffic when one zone becomes unavailable
explanation.additionalInfo: Availability Zones are the core building blocks of AWS high availability. Each AZ is physically separated and isolated to reduce the impact of failures. By deploying resources across multiple AZs, customers can build resilient and fault-tolerant architectures that withstand infrastructure failures.

questions.question: AWS provides disaster recovery capability by allowing customers to deploy infrastructure into multiple [...].

explanation.summary: Deploying infrastructure across multiple AWS Regions enables disaster recovery.
examples: Running active-passive workloads across two regions
Replicating data to a secondary region for DR
explanation.additionalInfo: AWS Regions are isolated geographic areas that consist of multiple Availability Zones. By deploying infrastructure across multiple Regions, customers can protect applications and data from large-scale events such as natural disasters or major outages. This regional isolation is the foundation of AWS disaster recovery architectures, including backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active-active strategies.

explanation.summary: Transportation devices are not part of AWS disaster recovery infrastructure.
explanation.why: AWS disaster recovery relies on cloud infrastructure components such as regions and Availability Zones, not physical transportation devices.

explanation.summary: Support plans do not provide disaster recovery capabilities.
explanation.why: AWS Support plans offer assistance and response times but do not affect infrastructure deployment or disaster recovery architecture.

explanation.summary: Edge locations are used for content delivery, not disaster recovery.
explanation.why: Edge locations support services like CloudFront for low-latency delivery but are not used to deploy full application infrastructure for disaster recovery.

questions.question: A financial services company decides to migrate one of its applications to AWS. The application deals with sensitive data, such as credit card information, and must run on a PCI-compliant environment. Which of the following is the company's responsibility when building a PCI-compliant environment in AWS? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Start the migration process immediately as all AWS services are PCI compliant.

explanation.summary: Not all AWS services are automatically PCI compliant by default.
explanation.why: While AWS infrastructure supports PCI DSS compliance, customers must select eligible services and configure them correctly to meet PCI requirements.

options.text: Ensure that AWS services are configured properly to meetall PCI DSS standards.

explanation.summary: Customers are responsible for configuring AWS services to meet PCI DSS requirements.
keyPoints: Includes network, access, and encryption controls
examples: Configuring security groups and network segmentation
Enabling encryption for cardholder data
explanation.additionalInfo: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, AWS is responsible for the security of the cloud, while customers are responsible for security in the cloud. This includes properly configuring AWS services to meet PCI DSS requirements, such as enforcing access controls, encrypting sensitive data, and maintaining secure network architectures.

options.text: Restrict any access to cardholder data and create a policy that addresses information security for all personnel.

explanation.summary: Restricting access and enforcing security policies is a customer responsibility.
keyPoints: Access to cardholder data must be limited
Security policies are required by PCI DSS
examples: Using IAM policies to restrict database access
Implementing internal security training and policies
explanation.additionalInfo: PCI DSS requires organizations to restrict access to cardholder data and maintain formal information security policies. In AWS, customers must design IAM policies, monitoring controls, and organizational processes to ensure only authorized personnel can access sensitive data. AWS does not manage these internal controls on behalf of the customer.

options.text: Configure the underlying infrastructure of AWS services to meet all PCI DSS requirements.

explanation.summary: AWS manages the underlying infrastructure for PCI compliance.
explanation.why: AWS is responsible for physical data centers, hardware, and underlying infrastructure security. Customers cannot configure these components directly.

options.text: Ensure that all PCI DSS physical security requirements are met.

explanation.summary: Physical security is AWS's responsibility.
explanation.why: AWS manages and audits physical data center security controls required for PCI DSS compliance.

questions.question: What is the maximum amount of data that can be stored in S3 in a single AWS account?

explanation.summary: Amazon S3 is not limited to 100 PB per account.
explanation.why: S3 is designed to scale far beyond fixed petabyte limits.

explanation.summary: Amazon S3 provides virtually unlimited object storage.
keyPoints: No predefined storage limits per account
Pay only for what you use
examples: Storing petabytes of analytics data
Archiving large-scale backup datasets
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon S3 is built to store and retrieve virtually unlimited amounts of data. Customers are not required to provision capacity in advance, and S3 automatically scales to meet demand. This makes it suitable for workloads ranging from small applications to massive data lakes.

explanation.summary: 5 TB refers to the maximum size of a single S3 object, not total storage.
explanation.why: While an individual S3 object can be up to 5 TB in size, total account storage is not limited to this value.

explanation.summary: Amazon S3 storage is not capped at a specific exabyte limit.
explanation.why: S3 is architected to scale beyond fixed capacity limits, making this option incorrect.

questions.question: Which pillar of the AWS Well-Architected Framework provides recommendations to help customers select the right compute resources based on workload requirements?

explanation.summary: Operational Excellence focuses on operations, not resource selection.
explanation.why: This pillar emphasizes monitoring, automation, and continuous improvement of operational processes rather than choosing compute types or performance characteristics.

explanation.summary: The Security pillar addresses protection of data and systems, not compute selection.
explanation.why: Security guidance focuses on identity, detection, infrastructure protection, and incident response rather than performance or resource sizing.

explanation.summary: Performance Efficiency provides guidance on selecting and using the right compute resources.
keyPoints: Focuses on efficient use of computing resources
Guides instance type and size selection
examples: Choosing memory-optimized instances for in-memory databases
Using serverless services to match demand automatically
explanation.additionalInfo: The Performance Efficiency pillar helps customers structure workloads to use resources efficiently. It emphasizes selecting the appropriate compute, storage, and networking resources based on workload requirements, adopting new technologies, and continuously monitoring performance to maintain efficiency as demand changes.

explanation.summary: Reliability focuses on fault tolerance and recovery, not compute sizing.
explanation.why: This pillar addresses resilience, failure handling, and recovery planning rather than selecting compute resources for performance needs.

questions.question: Which AWS service delivers data, videos, applications, and APIs to users globally with low latency and high transfer speeds?

explanation.summary: Amazon Route 53 is a DNS service, not a content delivery network.
explanation.why: Route 53 routes users to endpoints but does not cache or deliver content globally.

explanation.summary: Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center service.
explanation.why: It is used for customer service call centers, not content delivery.

explanation.summary: Amazon CloudFront is a global content delivery network.
keyPoints: Integrates with AWS Shield and WAF
examples: Serving videos to users worldwide
Delivering APIs closer to end users
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon CloudFront is AWS’s content delivery network that accelerates the delivery of websites, APIs, video content, and other assets to users globally. By caching content at edge locations close to users, CloudFront reduces latency and improves transfer speeds while providing integrated security features.

explanation.summary: Amazon EC2 provides compute capacity, not global content delivery.
explanation.why: EC2 instances host applications but do not provide a distributed edge network for low-latency delivery.

questions.question: Which of the following steps should be taken by a customer when conducting penetration testing on AWS?

options.text: Conduct penetration testing using Amazon Inspector, and then notify AWS support.

explanation.summary: Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability assessment service, not penetration testing approval.
explanation.why: Inspector does not replace formal penetration testing procedures or approval requirements.

options.text: Request and wait for approval from the customer's internal security team, and then conduct testing.

explanation.summary: Customers must follow internal approval processes before penetration testing.
keyPoints: AWS allows penetration testing on certain services
No AWS approval is required for permitted tests
examples: Security team approving a penetration test scope
Conducting tests on EC2 and RDS within allowed services
explanation.additionalInfo: AWS permits customers to perform penetration testing on their own resources without prior AWS approval, provided the testing is within allowed services and guidelines. Customers must still obtain internal authorization and ensure testing complies with AWS policies to avoid service disruption.

options.text: Notify AWS support, and then conduct testing immediately.

explanation.summary: Notifying AWS Support is not required for permitted penetration testing.
explanation.why: AWS does not require notification or approval for permitted tests, and testing should not begin without proper internal authorization.

options.text: Request and wait for approval from AWS support, and then conduct testing.

explanation.summary: AWS approval is not required for permitted penetration testing.
explanation.why: AWS has a published policy that allows penetration testing without requesting approval, making this option incorrect.

questions.question: Which AWS Cost Management tool allows you to view the most granular data about your AWS bill?

explanation.summary: AWS Cost Explorer provides summarized and visualized cost data.
explanation.why: Cost Explorer is designed for analysis and trend visualization. While it offers detailed views, it does not provide the most granular, line-item level billing data available in AWS.

explanation.summary: AWS Budgets is used for setting alerts, not detailed billing analysis.
explanation.why: Budgets tracks spending against defined thresholds and sends notifications. It does not expose detailed usage records.

explanation.summary: The AWS Cost and Usage Report provides the most detailed billing and usage data.
examples: Analyzing per-resource charges at hourly granularity
Feeding billing data into a data warehouse for reporting
explanation.additionalInfo: The AWS Cost and Usage Report is the most comprehensive billing dataset available. It contains detailed records of resource usage, pricing, and cost allocation tags. This report is commonly used for advanced cost analysis, chargeback models, and integration with business intelligence tools.

explanation.summary: The Billing dashboard provides high-level billing information.
explanation.why: The dashboard offers a summary of charges and trends but does not provide granular usage records.

questions.question: Which element of the AWS global infrastructure consists of one or more discrete data centers each with redundant power networking and connectivity which are housed in separate facilities?

explanation.summary: AWS Regions are geographic areas that contain multiple Availability Zones.
explanation.why: A Region is made up of multiple Availability Zones rather than individual data centers.

explanation.summary: Availability Zones consist of one or more discrete data centers.
keyPoints: Each AZ contains multiple data centers
examples: Deploying applications across two AZs
Failing over traffic between AZs
explanation.additionalInfo: Availability Zones are physically separate locations within an AWS Region, each composed of one or more data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity. This design minimizes the impact of failures and supports highly available and fault-tolerant architectures.

explanation.summary: Edge locations are used for content delivery, not core infrastructure.
explanation.why: Edge locations support services like CloudFront and Route 53 but do not host full application stacks or core AWS infrastructure.

explanation.summary: Amazon CloudFront is a CDN service, not an infrastructure element.
explanation.why: CloudFront uses edge locations but is not itself a component of the global infrastructure hierarchy.

questions.question: How many Availability Zones should compute resources be provisioned across to achieve high availability?

explanation.summary: Using a single Availability Zone does not provide high availability.
explanation.why: A single AZ represents a single point of failure at the zone level.

explanation.summary: At least two Availability Zones are required for high availability.
examples: Deploying EC2 instances in two AZs behind a load balancer
Using Multi-AZ database deployments
explanation.additionalInfo: High availability in AWS is achieved by deploying resources across multiple Availability Zones within a region. A minimum of two AZs ensures that applications can continue operating even if one zone becomes unavailable, making this a foundational design principle in AWS architectures.

explanation.summary: Three Availability Zones are not required for basic high availability.
explanation.why: While three AZs can improve resilience, AWS defines high availability as using at least two AZs.

options.text: A minimum of four or more.

explanation.summary: Four or more Availability Zones exceed the minimum requirement.
explanation.why: High availability can be achieved with two Availability Zones. Additional zones may improve resilience but are not mandatory.

questions.question: The AWS Cloud's multiple Regions are an example of:

explanation.summary: Agility refers to the ability to rapidly develop and deploy resources, not geographic distribution.
explanation.why: While AWS enables agility, multiple Regions specifically describe the geographic footprint of AWS infrastructure rather than development speed or flexibility.

explanation.summary: Multiple AWS Regions represent AWS's global infrastructure.
keyPoints: Regions are distributed across the world
Support disaster recovery and latency reduction
Each Region is isolated from others
examples: Deploying applications in multiple continents
Serving users with low latency using nearby Regions
explanation.additionalInfo: AWS global infrastructure consists of Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations. Regions are geographically separate areas that allow customers to deploy workloads close to end users and design for disaster recovery at a global scale. This worldwide footprint is a core differentiator of the AWS Cloud.

explanation.summary: Elasticity refers to scaling resources, not geographic distribution.
explanation.why: Elasticity is about scaling capacity up or down based on demand, whereas Regions describe physical locations.

explanation.summary: Pay-as-you-go pricing describes a billing model, not infrastructure layout.
explanation.why: While AWS uses pay-as-you-go pricing, multiple Regions reflect infrastructure distribution rather than cost structure.

questions.question: Which AWS service can be used to manually launch instances based on resource requirements?

explanation.summary: Amazon EBS provides block storage, not instance launch capabilities.
explanation.why: EBS volumes are attached to EC2 instances but cannot launch instances themselves.

explanation.summary: Amazon S3 is object storage and does not launch compute instances.
explanation.why: S3 stores data and does not provide compute provisioning functionality.

explanation.summary: Amazon EC2 allows users to manually launch instances with specific resource configurations.
keyPoints: Provides control over CPU, memory, and storage
examples: Launching a compute-optimized instance for batch processing
Selecting memory-optimized instances for in-memory workloads
explanation.additionalInfo: Amazon EC2 provides full control over instance configuration, allowing customers to manually select instance types, storage options, networking settings, and purchasing models. This flexibility makes EC2 suitable for workloads with specific resource requirements or custom configurations.

explanation.summary: Amazon ECS orchestrates containers rather than launching raw EC2 instances manually.
explanation.why: ECS manages containerized workloads and abstracts instance management when using managed compute options.

questions.question: Which is a recommended pattern for designing a highly available architecture on AWS?

options.text: Ensure that components have low-latency network connectivity.

explanation.summary: Low latency improves performance but does not guarantee high availability.
explanation.why: High availability focuses on fault tolerance and resilience rather than network speed alone.

options.text: Run enough Amazon EC2 instances to operate at peak load.

explanation.summary: Provisioning for peak load does not ensure fault tolerance.
explanation.why: High availability requires designing for failure, not just capacity planning.

options.text: Ensure that the application is designed to accommodate failure of any single component.

explanation.summary: Designing for failure is a core principle of high availability on AWS.
examples: Using load balancers to route around failed instances
Deploying stateless application tiers
explanation.additionalInfo: Highly available architectures on AWS are built by assuming failure as a normal condition. Applications should be designed so that the failure of any single component does not cause a system-wide outage. This includes using redundancy, health checks, automated recovery, and decoupled architectures.

options.text: Use a monolithic application that handles all operations.

explanation.summary: Monolithic designs increase the impact of failures.
explanation.why: A monolithic architecture can create single points of failure and reduce fault isolation.

questions.question: Which AWS characteristics make AWS cost effective for a workload with dynamic user demand? (Select TWO)

explanation.summary: High availability improves resilience but does not directly reduce cost for dynamic demand.
explanation.why: High availability focuses on fault tolerance and uptime. Cost effectiveness for dynamic workloads comes from scaling and pricing flexibility, not redundancy alone.

explanation.summary: The shared responsibility model defines security ownership, not cost efficiency.
